input.description: List proteins in the ferritin, RNR-like, and Mn catalase families

toolu_01C2eW99JXLYp1dfyu9nyufu.description: List proteins in the ferritin, RNR-like, and Mn catalase families

content.text: I have everything needed. The current release is 2.08, and the three groups are sibling families inside one superfamily. Here is the answer.

answers.answer:
In SCOPe 2.08 (the current release; frozen 2021-07-28, released 2021-09-22) ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins, and manganese catalases are three sibling families of ONE superfamily, a.25.1 'Ferritin-like' (sunid 47240), within fold a.25 'Ferritin-like' (sunid 47239) in class a (all-alpha). The families are a.25.1.1 'Ferritin' (sunid 47241), a.25.1.2 'Ribonucleotide reductase-like' (sunid 47253), and a.25.1.3 'Manganese catalase (T-catalase)' (sunid 100951, mapped to Pfam PF05067). The superfamily also holds YciF-like (a.25.1.4), half-ferritin (a.25.1.5), PMT1231-like (a.25.1.6), MiaE-like (a.25.1.7), AMB4284-like (a.25.1.8), Rv2844-like (a.25.1.9) and an 'automated matches' family a.25.1.0.

How to read this at each level. (1) Superfamily = SCOPe's assertion of probable common ancestry despite low sequence identity. The curators' comment on a.25.1 states the shared, non-trivial feature: it 'contains bimetal-ion centre in the middle of the bundle'. So the homology argument is not just a four-helix bundle; it is a conserved di-metal site (ferroxidase-type Glu/His ligands on the helices) occupying the same position in the bundle, which is the kind of functional-site conservation SCOP uses as evidence of divergence from a common ancestor rather than convergence. The different chemistries are therefore interpreted as functional divergence of one ancestral di-metal-binding scaffold: ferritins (a.25.1.1: apoferritin, bacterioferritin, Dps 'dodecameric ferritin homolog', rubrerythrin/nigerythrin N-terminal domains, non-heme ferritin) use a di-iron ferroxidase centre for Fe(II) oxidation and iron storage; RNR-like proteins (a.25.1.2: RNR R2, methane monooxygenase alpha and beta subunits, toluene/o-xylene monooxygenase TouA/TouE, delta-9 stearoyl-ACP desaturase, PaaC) use di-iron (or Mn/Fe) centres for radical generation and O2 activation; manganese catalases (a.25.1.3) use a di-manganese centre for H2O2 disproportionation. Same site, same scaffold, different metal/redox chemistry. (2) Family = the level at which function and detailed mechanism are reasonably transferable (clear sequence/structure similarity). Chemistry should only be inferred within a family, and even within a.25.1.2 the members span monooxygenases, desaturases, and a reductase subunit, so a family label does not fix substrate. (3) Fold a.25 is defined purely geometrically ('core: 4 helices; bundle, closed, left-handed twist; 1 crossover connection'); the other superfamilies in this fold, cobalamin adenosyltransferase-like (a.25.2), EsxAB dimer-like (a.25.3), PE/PPE dimer-like (a.25.4), HP0062-like (a.25.5), SO2669-like (a.25.6), share the bundle but NOT the bimetal centre and are not claimed to be homologous to ferritins. Fold-level similarity carries no inference about ancestry or catalysis. (4) Class a merely says all-alpha.

Limits. Superfamily membership supports 'homologous di-metal scaffold' but does not license transferring catalytic activity, metal preference (Fe vs Mn), oxidation state, substrate, or oligomeric state (24-mer ferritin cage, 12-mer Dps, hexameric Mn catalase, R2 dimer) between families; these are exactly what diverged. A ferritin or Mn-catalase structure is a usable template for the helical bundle core and the approximate metal-site position of an RNR-like protein, but not for active-site loops, second-shell residues, or quaternary assembly. Many members are classified as 'automated matches' (a.25.1.0 and per-family automated-match protein nodes), i.e. assigned by sequence to a curated family without manual review, so family placement of those domains should be treated as provisional. Note also that the SCOPe node a.25.1.3 is called 'Manganese catalase (T-catalase)', a different fold and chemistry from heme catalases, which SCOPe places in e.5.1.1 (e.g. d7catb_) and which are unrelated. To go beyond SCOPe's homology claim and actually assign chemistry to a new ferritin-like domain one needs external evidence: conserved metal-ligand motifs in a sequence alignment, metal content/EPR or crystallographic metal identification, and biochemical assay of ferroxidase, catalase, or oxygenase activity.
evidence_used: pretrained knowledge of ferritin-like di-metal site chemistry
